text: 11 A retrospective review of patients given salvage therapy with voriconazole plus caspofungin or voriconazole alone reported that 3-month survival was greater for the combination than for voriconazole alone.12 Successful treatment for invasive aspergillosis was also described in 2 patients who received a combination of caspofungin and itraconazole.13 Treatment for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis should be given for a minimum of 6 to 12 weeks; in immunosuppressed patients, it should be continued throughout the period of immunosuppression and until the lesions have cleared.11 In neutropenic patients with prolonged fever despite broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy, empirical treatment with amphotericin B or its lipid formulations, itraconazole, voriconazole, or caspofungin is recommended.11 Antifungal prophylaxis with posaconazole is recommend- ed for haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients with graft-versus-host disease and in patients with acute mye- loid leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndromes who are at high risk for invasive aspergillosis. Itraconazole may be useful, but it is not well tolerated.1,11,14 Non-invasive forms of aspergillosis include allergic bron- chopulmonary aspergillosis, a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus usually occurring in asthmatic patients, and as- pergilloma, a fungal mass or ball developing within a pre- existing pulmonary cavity or paranasal sinus. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is usually treated with corticosteroids and oral itraconazole.11,15 A systematic review16 has concluded that itraconazole modifies the im- munological activation associated with allergic bronchop- ulmonary aspergillosis in asthmatic patients and improves clinical outcome in the first 4 months of treatment. The treatment of aspergilloma depends on the severity of symptoms, and includes conservative management, anti- fungal therapy, or surgical resection. Treatment with itra- conazole, voriconazole, and possibly also posaconazole are considered to have some benefit. Surgical resection and direct intracavitary instillation of antifungals may also be useful in selected patients with a single aspergilloma.11 Chronic necrotising pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA or subacute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis)17 is a subacute infection seen in patients with an underlying lung disease or systemic risk factors for immunosuppression. Various antifungals have been tried in the treatment of CNPA. Case reports have shown amphotericin B to be successful in about 50% of the patients and clinical benefit has also been achieved with intracavitary amphotericin B.
